title: AWS Serverless and Containers: Lambda, API Gateway, ECS, EKS, Fargate and Event-Driven Glue
intro: AWS offers three compute models on a spectrum of responsibility: virtual machines (EC2), containers (ECR, ECS, EKS, Fargate) and serverless functions (Lambda), each trading control for less operational work. The goal of this lesson is to understand what you manage in each model, how the core services work, and how to choose and combine them, ending with a complete serverless image-processing pipeline.

sections.heading: The compute spectrum: what you manage in each model
sections.content:
Every compute choice on AWS answers one question: how much of the stack do you want to run yourself? Think of three ways to get a meal. Renting a kitchen (EC2) gives you full control and full cleanup. Ordering a meal kit (containers) gives you a standard box and someone else's stove. Ordering delivery (serverless) means you only specify the dish and pay per meal.

**EC2 (virtual machines).** You pick an instance type, an AMI and a network placement, and you own everything above the hypervisor: OS patching, runtime installation, agents, scaling groups, capacity planning. You pay per second (Linux) while the instance runs, whether it is busy or idle. Choose it for legacy software, special hardware (GPUs, large memory), licensing constraints, or very steady and heavy workloads where reserved capacity is cheapest.

**Containers.** A container packages your code with its dependencies into an image that runs the same everywhere. You still decide how many copies run and how much CPU and memory each gets, but you no longer hand-install runtimes on hosts. Containers can run on EC2 hosts you manage, or on Fargate, where AWS manages the hosts.

**Serverless (Lambda).** You upload a function. AWS provisions execution environments on demand, scales them from zero to thousands, and bills only for the milliseconds your code actually runs. You manage code, configuration (memory, timeout, permissions) and event wiring, nothing below that.

| Aspect | EC2 | Containers (ECS/EKS) | Serverless (Lambda) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unit of deployment | AMI / instance | Container image | Function code or image |
| You patch the OS | Yes | Yes on EC2 hosts, no on Fargate | No |
| Scaling | Auto Scaling groups, minutes | Service scaling, tens of seconds to minutes | Automatic, per request, milliseconds to seconds |
| Idle cost | Pay while running | Pay while tasks run | Zero when no invocations |
| Max run time | Unlimited | Unlimited | 15 minutes per invocation |
| Startup latency | Minutes | Seconds | Cold start up to about a second or more |
| Best for | Legacy, special hardware, steady heavy load | Long-running services, microservices | Event-driven, spiky, glue logic |

The shared responsibility model shifts accordingly. With EC2 the customer secures the guest OS and everything above. With Fargate and Lambda, AWS takes the OS and host layer, and the customer still owns code, dependencies, IAM permissions and data. A frequent beginner mistake is thinking serverless means no security work: your function's role, your dependencies and your event inputs are all yours.

**What to ask:** How long does a unit of work run? Is traffic steady or spiky? Do we need a specific OS, library set or hardware? Who will be on call for patching? The rest of this lesson maps those answers to concrete services.

sections.heading: AWS Lambda: event-driven functions and the execution model
sections.content:
Lambda runs a function in response to an event. A trigger (also called an event source) produces an event, Lambda hands it to your handler, and the handler returns. Triggers fall into three families:

- **Synchronous:** the caller waits for the answer. API Gateway, Application Load Balancer and direct SDK invokes work this way. Errors go back to the caller.
- **Asynchronous:** the caller hands off and leaves. S3, SNS and EventBridge use this. Lambda queues the event and retries failures twice by default, and you can attach a dead-letter queue or an on-failure destination.
- **Poll-based (event source mapping):** Lambda itself polls SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams or Kafka and invokes your function with batches of records.

**The execution model.** Lambda runs your code inside an execution environment, a small isolated sandbox. The first invocation in a new environment goes through an init phase: download the code, start the runtime, run code outside the handler. That is the **cold start**, typically tens to hundreds of milliseconds for Node.js or Python and often longer for Java or .NET or for large packages. After the invoke, the environment is kept warm for a while and reused, so later invocations skip init. Each environment handles exactly one request at a time.

**Concurrency** follows from that rule. If 300 requests arrive at the same instant, Lambda needs 300 environments, so concurrency is 300. The default regional account limit is 1,000 concurrent executions (a soft limit you can raise). Two controls matter:

- **Reserved concurrency** caps and guarantees a function's share, which protects both the function and the downstream database it calls.
- **Provisioned concurrency** keeps environments pre-initialized so latency-sensitive paths avoid cold starts, at an hourly cost.

**Configuration knobs.** You set memory from 128 MB up to 10,240 MB, and CPU scales proportionally with memory, so a CPU-bound function often runs cheaper at higher memory because it finishes faster. The maximum timeout is 900 seconds (15 minutes). Synchronous payloads are limited to about 6 MB, local /tmp space defaults to 512 MB, and a zip package is limited to 50 MB zipped and 250 MB unzipped (container-image functions go up to 10 GB).

**Pricing** has two parts: a per-request charge (roughly 20 cents per million requests) and a duration charge in GB-seconds, which is memory multiplied by billed time. A monthly free tier covers the first million requests and 400,000 GB-seconds. Idle costs nothing, which makes Lambda superb for spiky work and expensive for a function that runs hot 24/7.

```python
import json

# Code outside the handler runs once per cold start: reuse clients here
counter = {'calls': 0}

def handler(event, context):
    counter['calls'] += 1
    return {
        'statusCode': 200,
        'body': json.dumps({'calls_in_this_environment': counter['calls'],
                            'time_left_ms': context.get_remaining_time_in_millis()})
    }
```

**Pitfalls:** treating the 15-minute timeout as a design target, opening database connections per invocation and exhausting the database during a burst, and forgetting that async retries mean your function can run twice for the same event, so it must be idempotent.

Security note: execution roles and iam:PassRole abuse are covered in the existing cloud IAM lesson.

sections.heading: API Gateway and the serverless web pattern
sections.content:
API Gateway is the managed front door for HTTP-style APIs. It terminates TLS, routes requests by method and path, applies throttling, authorizes callers and forwards to a backend. Think of it as a receptionist: it checks who you are, how often you have visited, and which office you need, and only then calls the right person.

**API types.**

- **REST API:** the feature-rich option. It adds request validation, usage plans and API keys, caching, WAF integration, request and response transformation, and private endpoints.
- **HTTP API:** a leaner, cheaper and faster product aimed at proxying to Lambda or HTTP backends, with built-in JWT authorizers. Most new simple APIs start here.
- **WebSocket API:** persistent two-way connections for chat or live dashboards.

**Integrations.** The common choice is Lambda proxy integration: API Gateway packages the whole HTTP request (method, path, headers, query string, body) into the event, and your function returns a status code, headers and body. The gateway does no transformation, so your code owns the contract.

**Authorization options:** IAM (SigV4 signed requests, good for service-to-service), Amazon Cognito user pools or JWT authorizers (end users), and Lambda authorizers (custom logic, for example validating a partner token).

**The serverless web pattern.** A classic three-tier app with no servers to patch:

```text
Browser -> CloudFront/S3 (static front end)
       -> API Gateway (HTTPS, auth, throttling)
       -> Lambda (business logic)
       -> DynamoDB (single-digit millisecond key-value store)
```

Each layer scales independently and bills per use, so a site with ten visitors a day costs almost nothing, and the same stack survives a traffic spike without capacity planning.

**Pitfalls worth memorizing:**

- **Time limit.** API Gateway's integration timeout is around 29 seconds for REST APIs and 30 seconds for HTTP APIs. A Lambda that can run 15 minutes still cannot keep a synchronous HTTP request open that long. Long work needs the accept-then-process pattern: return 202 with a job ID, enqueue the work, let the client poll or receive a callback.
- **Throttling chain.** API Gateway throttles, Lambda concurrency throttles and DynamoDB capacity throttles. A burst can be rejected at any hop, so set limits deliberately and return clear 429 responses.
- **Cold start on the user path.** Interactive endpoints feel cold starts. Use lightweight runtimes, small packages, provisioned concurrency where it matters, and lazy initialization.
- **DynamoDB design.** It is not a relational database. You model access patterns first (partition key and sort key), because scans over large tables are slow and costly.

**What to ask:** What is the p99 latency target? Which hop enforces authentication? What happens when the database throttles? Is any request allowed to take longer than 29 seconds?

sections.heading: Containers on AWS: images, ECR, ECS and launch types
sections.content:
A **container image** is an immutable, layered file system snapshot plus startup metadata, built from a Dockerfile. A **container** is a running instance of that image, isolated by the kernel (namespaces and cgroups) but sharing the host kernel, which is why containers start in seconds and are far lighter than VMs. The promise is build once, run identically on a laptop, in CI and in production.

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
USER 1000
CMD python server.py
```

**ECR (Elastic Container Registry)** is AWS's private image registry. You push images with tags (and should deploy by immutable digest or unique tag, not latest). ECR integrates with IAM for pull and push permissions, offers image scanning for known vulnerabilities, lifecycle policies to expire old images and cross-region replication. Lambda container images also live here.

**ECS (Elastic Container Service)** is AWS's own orchestrator. Its vocabulary is small:

- **Task definition:** the blueprint, like a recipe. It lists one or more containers, their image, CPU and memory, ports, environment variables, logging config, and the IAM roles.
- **Task:** one running instance of a task definition.
- **Service:** keeps N tasks running, replaces failed ones, performs rolling deployments and registers tasks with a load balancer.
- **Cluster:** the logical grouping of capacity.

Two IAM roles confuse beginners: the **task execution role** lets ECS itself pull the image from ECR and write logs, while the **task role** is what your application code uses to call AWS APIs such as S3.

**Launch types: Fargate vs EC2.** This is the real decision about who runs the hosts.

| Aspect | Fargate | EC2 launch type |
|---|---|---|
| Hosts | AWS-managed, invisible | You run and patch the instances |
| Billing | Per vCPU-second and GB-second of the task | Per instance, whether full or not |
| Scaling | Add tasks, capacity appears | Scale tasks and the instance fleet |
| Isolation | Each task in its own micro-VM | Tasks share instances |
| Special needs (GPU, huge memory, daemons, host access) | Limited | Supported |
| Cost at high steady utilization | Higher | Lower, especially with reservations or Spot |
| Operational burden | Low | Higher |

A sensible default is Fargate first, and move to EC2 only when you can prove a cost or hardware need. Packing instances at 80 percent utilization with Savings Plans beats Fargate on price, but a half-empty cluster you must also patch does not.

**Pitfalls:** running as root in the image, pulling the latest tag so deployments are not reproducible, putting secrets in environment variables in plain text instead of referencing Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, and sizing tasks too small so they are killed for out-of-memory.

sections.heading: EKS at a glance and when to choose it over ECS
sections.content:
**EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service)** is managed Kubernetes. AWS runs and patches the control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler) across multiple Availability Zones, and you run workloads on worker capacity that you attach. Kubernetes is the open-source industry standard orchestrator, with a very large ecosystem of tools, operators and skills.

Kubernetes has its own vocabulary: a **pod** is the smallest unit (one or more containers), a **deployment** keeps N replicas of a pod running, a **service** gives pods a stable address, an **ingress** routes external traffic, and **namespaces** divide a cluster. Configuration is declared in YAML manifests and applied with kubectl or a GitOps tool.

**Worker options in EKS:**

- **Managed node groups:** EC2 instances AWS provisions and upgrades for you.
- **Self-managed nodes:** maximum control, maximum effort.
- **Fargate profiles:** pods run on serverless capacity, with no nodes to patch, though with some limitations (for example, no DaemonSets and no GPUs).
- **Karpenter or Auto Mode:** automatic node provisioning sized to pending pods.

The control plane carries a flat hourly fee per cluster (on the order of 10 cents an hour), on top of the compute you use. ECS has no control plane charge.

| Aspect | ECS | EKS |
|---|---|---|
| Technology | AWS-proprietary, simple | Open-source Kubernetes |
| Learning curve | Gentle: tasks, services | Steep: pods, controllers, networking, RBAC |
| Portability | AWS only | Same manifests run on other clouds and on-premises |
| Ecosystem | AWS-integrated | Huge: Helm, operators, service meshes, CNCF tools |
| Control plane cost | None | Per-cluster hourly fee |
| Ops overhead | Low | Higher: version upgrades, add-ons, cluster security |
| Typical fit | Teams that want containers running quickly | Organizations standardized on Kubernetes |

**When to choose EKS:** the organization already has Kubernetes skills and tooling, you need multi-cloud or hybrid portability, you depend on Kubernetes-native tools (operators, Helm charts, service mesh), or you run a large platform serving many teams that needs namespaces, policies and a rich API.

**When ECS is the better answer:** a small team, a handful of services, deep AWS integration needed, and no existing Kubernetes investment. For most first container workloads ECS on Fargate is the lowest-effort path.

**Pitfall: over-using Kubernetes.** Teams adopt it because it is fashionable, then spend months on cluster upgrades (Kubernetes releases a minor version every few months and old versions go out of support), ingress controllers, network policies and RBAC for an app that would have run happily on ECS or even Lambda. Kubernetes is a platform for building platforms. If you cannot name a feature you need that ECS lacks, you probably do not need it.

**What to ask:** Who will upgrade the cluster? Do we need to leave AWS someday for real, or is portability just a comfort? Do we have the people to operate it?

sections.heading: Orchestration and messaging: Step Functions, SQS, SNS and EventBridge
sections.content:
Serverless systems are built from small pieces that must talk without being tightly bound. Coupling is the enemy: if service A calls service B directly, then B being slow or down breaks A. Messaging services put a buffer or a router between them, which is called **decoupling**.

**SQS (Simple Queue Service)** is a durable queue. Producers send messages, consumers poll and process them. Key ideas:

- **Buffering:** a burst of 50,000 messages is absorbed by the queue while consumers work at a safe rate.
- **Visibility timeout:** when a consumer receives a message it is hidden for a period. If the consumer does not delete it in time, it reappears. Set it longer than your processing time (for Lambda consumers, at least six times the function timeout is the recommended rule).
- **Dead-letter queue (DLQ):** after N failed receives a message moves to a DLQ so one poison message cannot block everything, and you can inspect it later.
- **Standard vs FIFO:** standard queues give at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering with nearly unlimited throughput; FIFO queues guarantee order within a message group and deduplicate, at lower throughput.

**SNS (Simple Notification Service)** is publish and subscribe. A publisher sends one message to a topic, and every subscriber (SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTPS endpoints, email, SMS) receives a copy. The famous **fan-out** pattern is SNS topic to several SQS queues, so each consumer processes the same event independently at its own pace.

**EventBridge** is an event bus with rule-based routing. Events from AWS services, your own applications or SaaS partners arrive on a bus, and rules with JSON pattern matching send matching events to targets. It also offers schedules (cron-like jobs that replace a server running cron) and a schema registry. Choose EventBridge when routing depends on event content and many producers or consumers exist; choose SNS for simple high-throughput fan-out; choose SQS when you need a work queue with retries.

**Step Functions** orchestrates multi-step workflows as a state machine defined in Amazon States Language (JSON). It provides sequencing, branching (Choice), parallel branches, Map for iterating over items, waiting (up to a year in Standard), and built-in Retry and Catch with backoff. Instead of one giant Lambda that calls others and tracks its own state, the workflow engine records every step.

- **Standard workflows:** up to one year, exactly-once execution semantics, full execution history, priced per state transition.
- **Express workflows:** up to five minutes, very high rate, at-least-once, priced by count and duration, best for high-volume event processing.

```text
Choice: is the order valid?
  yes -> Task: charge card (Retry 3x, backoff)
      -> Task: reserve stock
          Catch -> Task: refund card -> Fail
      -> Task: send confirmation -> Succeed
  no  -> Fail
```

This example shows why orchestration matters: the refund compensation step is explicit and visible, not hidden in nested try blocks.

**Pitfalls:** assuming exactly-once delivery from SQS standard or SNS (you must write idempotent consumers), a visibility timeout shorter than the processing time (duplicate processing), and forgetting a DLQ so failures disappear silently.

sections.heading: Choosing: a decision guide
sections.content:
There is no best service, only a best fit for a workload shape. Start by classifying the workload, then pick the simplest model that satisfies it.

**1. Steady, long-running service** (an internal API with constant traffic, a web app, a database proxy). Traffic is predictable and the process runs all day. Lambda billing per millisecond becomes expensive at constant high load, and cold starts add no value. Choose **ECS on Fargate** for low operational effort, **ECS on EC2** when utilization is high and you want the lowest unit price, or **EKS** if the organization is a Kubernetes shop. Use EC2 directly for legacy or special hardware.

**2. Spiky or event-driven work** (react to file uploads, webhooks, queue messages, schedules, IoT events, low-traffic APIs). Idle periods are long and bursts are short. Choose **Lambda** with the right trigger. You pay nothing between events and scale instantly without planning.

**3. Batch and long jobs** (video transcoding of long files, nightly ETL, machine learning training). Runs that exceed 15 minutes or need lots of memory, disk or GPUs do not fit Lambda. Choose **Fargate tasks** launched on a schedule or an event, **AWS Batch** for queues of jobs, or Step Functions coordinating many short Lambda steps through a Map state when the job can be sliced into chunks.

| Workload shape | First choice | Why | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Steady API, 24/7 | ECS Fargate (or EC2 for savings) | Predictable cost, no time limit | Paying for idle headroom |
| Spiky or event-driven | Lambda | Scale to zero, per-request billing | Cold starts, concurrency limits |
| Long batch | Fargate task or AWS Batch | No 15-minute limit | Startup time, job retry design |
| Org on Kubernetes | EKS | Portability, ecosystem | Upgrade and ops burden |
| Legacy or GPU | EC2 | Full control | Patching and capacity |

**Rules of thumb that hold up in practice:**

- Prefer the highest abstraction that meets the requirement. Lambda, then Fargate, then EC2 is the order of increasing responsibility.
- Do the arithmetic. A function running 100 million times a month at 200 ms and 512 MB may cost more than a small always-on container. A function invoked 20,000 times a day costs pennies. Check the pricing calculator rather than guessing.
- Mixed architectures are normal: a Fargate service for the core API, Lambda for image resizing and scheduled cleanup, SQS between them, Step Functions for the ordering workflow.
- Avoid premature Kubernetes and premature microservices. A modular single service on ECS is easier to operate than twenty functions that call each other synchronously.
- Watch the hidden constraints: Lambda in a VPC needs the right subnets and NAT or endpoints to reach the internet and AWS APIs, and container tasks need image pull access to ECR.

**What to ask before deciding:** How long does one unit of work run? What is the peak-to-average traffic ratio? What latency can users tolerate on the first request? Who operates this at 3 AM? What does it cost at 10 times the load?

sections.heading: Worked example: a serverless image-processing pipeline
sections.content:
**Requirement:** users upload photos, and the system must create a thumbnail, record metadata and notify the owner. Uploads are bursty (a marketing campaign may send thousands in minutes) and the platform is idle at night. That is the textbook serverless shape.

```text
S3 (uploads bucket)
  -> event notification -> SQS queue (buffer, DLQ attached)
  -> Lambda (resize, write)
       -> S3 (thumbnails bucket)
       -> DynamoDB (image metadata table)
       -> SNS topic (image-processed) -> email, other consumers
```

**Piece by piece.**

1. **S3 uploads bucket.** Durable object storage, the source of events. Users upload through short-lived pre-signed URLs so the file never travels through your servers.
2. **Event notification to SQS.** S3 can invoke Lambda directly, but putting a queue in the middle gives buffering, retry control and a DLQ. If a thousand files land at once, the queue absorbs the spike and Lambda concurrency stays bounded, which also protects DynamoDB.
3. **Lambda function.** Reads the object, resizes it, writes the result. Give it generous memory (1,024 MB or more for image libraries, since CPU scales with memory), a timeout comfortably above the worst-case image (for example 60 seconds), and an SQS visibility timeout of at least six times that.
4. **Thumbnails bucket.** A separate bucket (or at least a separate prefix with a filtered trigger). Writing output into the bucket that triggers the function creates an infinite loop and a very surprising bill. This is the most common mistake in this pattern.
5. **DynamoDB table.** Stores image ID (partition key), owner, original key, thumbnail key, size and timestamp. Key-value lookups stay fast at any scale and cost nothing while idle.
6. **SNS topic.** Publishes an image-processed event. Today the subscriber is an email or a notification service; tomorrow you can add an analytics queue or a moderation function without touching the resize code. That is decoupling paying off.

```python
import boto3, json, io, urllib.parse
from PIL import Image

s3 = boto3.client('s3')
db = boto3.resource('dynamodb').Table('image-metadata')
sns = boto3.client('sns')

def handler(event, context):
    for record in event['Records']:
        body = json.loads(record['body'])
        for rec in body.get('Records', []):
            bucket = rec['s3']['bucket']['name']
            key = urllib.parse.unquote_plus(rec['s3']['object']['key'])
            raw = s3.get_object(Bucket=bucket, Key=key)['Body'].read()
            img = Image.open(io.BytesIO(raw))
            img.thumbnail((256, 256))
            out = io.BytesIO()
            img.save(out, format='JPEG')
            thumb_key = 'thumbs/' + key
            s3.put_object(Bucket='photos-thumbnails', Key=thumb_key, Body=out.getvalue())
            db.put_item(Item={'image_id': key, 'thumb': thumb_key, 'bytes': len(raw)})
            sns.publish(TopicArn='arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:111122223333:image-processed',
                        Message='processed ' + key)
```

Note the details: object keys arrive URL-encoded, so decode them; the write to DynamoDB with the same key is naturally idempotent, so a duplicate delivery just overwrites the same item; and SDK clients are created outside the handler so warm invocations reuse them.

**Failure handling.** A corrupt image raises an exception, the message returns to the queue after the visibility timeout, and after a few attempts it moves to the DLQ where an alarm on queue depth alerts the team. Nothing is lost and one bad file does not stop the line.

**Operations.** Each function logs to CloudWatch Logs, and you alarm on errors, throttles, duration near the timeout, and DLQ depth. Grant the Lambda role only the specific actions on the specific resources it uses.

**Cost shape:** zero when no one uploads, and proportional to uploads otherwise. If load later becomes huge and steady, or images exceed what 15 minutes allows, you can swap the processing step to a Fargate worker reading the same queue without changing anything upstream. That swap is possible only because the queue decoupled the stages.

quiz.question: A team has a containerized API on ECS. They want no EC2 instances to patch or scale, and they do not need GPUs or host-level access. Which launch type fits best?

options.label: EC2 launch type, because it always costs less than any alternative
Fargate, because AWS manages the underlying hosts and bills per task vCPU and memory
Lambda, because ECS tasks can only be run by invoking functions
EKS managed node groups, because ECS cannot run without Kubernetes

quiz.explanation: Fargate removes host management: AWS provisions and patches the underlying capacity, and you pay per task for the vCPU and memory it uses. That matches a team that wants no instances to maintain and has no special hardware needs. The EC2 launch type is not always cheaper (it only wins at high, steady utilization) and it brings patching duties. ECS tasks are not run by invoking Lambda functions. ECS is its own orchestrator and does not require Kubernetes or node groups.

quiz.question: A Lambda function transcodes uploaded videos and some files take about 25 minutes. The function times out. What is the correct diagnosis and fix?

options.label: Increase memory to 10 GB, which removes the timeout entirely
Add provisioned concurrency so the function never cold starts and never times out
Lambda's maximum is 15 minutes, so move the work to a Fargate task or Batch, or split it into chunks
Put the function behind API Gateway, which extends the timeout to one hour

quiz.explanation: Lambda has a hard 900 second (15 minute) maximum per invocation, so a 25 minute job cannot succeed no matter how it is configured. The fix is architectural: run it on Fargate or AWS Batch, or slice the video into pieces processed by many short invocations coordinated by Step Functions. More memory only speeds up CPU and does not lift the limit. Provisioned concurrency addresses cold starts, not run time. API Gateway has its own timeout of about 29 to 30 seconds and does not extend anything.

quiz.question: An order service must keep accepting orders during traffic bursts and when the downstream billing service is briefly unavailable, without losing messages. Which design best achieves this?

options.label: Put an SQS queue between them, with a dead-letter queue for repeatedly failing messages
Have the order service call billing synchronously and retry in a tight loop
Publish to an SNS topic with an email subscriber, so billing is notified
Increase the order service's Lambda timeout to 15 minutes so it can wait for billing

quiz.explanation: A queue decouples the two services: orders are stored durably, billing consumes at its own pace, failures are retried via the visibility timeout, and poison messages land in a DLQ for inspection. A synchronous call with tight retries couples the services and amplifies the outage. An email subscriber is a notification, not a durable work buffer. Waiting up to 15 minutes ties up concurrency, costs money while idle and still loses work if the function fails.

quiz.question: A company with five developers is deploying its first three containerized services on AWS. Which statement about choosing between ECS and EKS is most accurate?

options.label: EKS is always the better choice because Kubernetes is more modern than ECS
ECS cannot run containers on Fargate, so EKS is required for serverless containers
EKS has no control plane fee, so it is cheaper than ECS in every case
ECS is usually simpler to start with, and EKS pays off when you need Kubernetes tooling or portability

quiz.explanation: With a small team and no Kubernetes investment, ECS (often on Fargate) gets services running with the least operational overhead. EKS becomes attractive when the organization already uses Kubernetes, needs its ecosystem, or wants portability across environments. EKS is not automatically better, and it adds cluster upgrades and a per-cluster hourly control plane fee. ECS fully supports Fargate, so serverless containers do not require EKS.

quiz.question: Users of a Lambda-backed API notice that the first request after a quiet period is slow, while later requests are fast. Which explanation and mitigation are right?

options.label: API Gateway caches the first response, so reduce its TTL to zero
A cold start initialized a new environment, so use provisioned concurrency or trim the package and init code
DynamoDB is out of capacity after idle time, so switch the table to a bigger instance size
The function exceeded reserved concurrency, so raise the memory setting to remove throttling

quiz.explanation: Slow first request after idle and fast follow-ups is the signature of a cold start: Lambda had to create an environment, load the code and run init logic. Provisioned concurrency keeps environments ready, and smaller packages, lighter runtimes and lazy initialization reduce init time. API Gateway does not behave this way by default. DynamoDB tables are not sized as instances, and throttling shows up as errors rather than a slow first call. Throttling from concurrency limits produces 429 errors, and memory does not change a concurrency limit.
